title: TSAAT Overview
subtitle: See the terrain. Understand the connections.
intro: A connected view of the devices, software, networks and services that Defence relies on.
sourceNote: The programme timeline follows the history supplied for this guide. Diagrams are illustrative, not live Defence data.

sections.title: What is TSAAT?
body: The Threat Surface Area Assessment Tool (TSAAT) brings recorded observations about the cyber terrain together to create a context aware data set to explore and report on.
TSAAT assists cyber teams in governing the cyber posture of the Defence Cyber Terrain (DCT) and reducing the threat surface area of networks and ICT systems.
sections.takeaway: Understand the Cyber Terrain. Investigate an issue or finding. Turn insights into a report.

film.headline: Turn observations into context.
film.body: Bring recorded observations about devices, software, networks and services into a context aware data set.

film.headline: Connect the cyber terrain.
film.body: Explore how ICT systems support mission services and business services.

film.headline: Support the next decision.
film.body: Help cyber teams govern the posture of the Defence Cyber Terrain and reduce the threat surface area of networks and ICT systems.

sections.title: Where did it come from?
sections.lead: Built on discovery. Shaped by assessment.
body: TSAAT grew from Defence's work to discover and model its ICT environment, then assess the threat surface of critical systems.
Select a milestone to follow the journey from the 2019 discovery project to the planned next release.
sections.takeaway: Discovery provided the foundation for a wider view of the terrain.

film.body: A CMDB and dynamic discovery foundation, followed by configuration management and ICT system modelling.
Critical system assessments, DIIS ownership records, OMWOW modelling and TSAAT V2.0.

film.headline: 2026 → planned January 2027
film.body: DSOC and Cyber Command engagement informs the design of TSAAT V3.0.

sections.kicker: More than a list of assets
sections.title: What is the cyber terrain?
sections.lead: The digital environment your work depends on.
body: Cyber terrain includes devices, installed software, networks, ICT systems, mission services and business services, together with their recorded relationships.
Explore this illustrative topology of three networks and 18 device configuration items (CIs). Select a layer to highlight its components, or show all components to see the connected picture.
sections.takeaway: Understand the parts and how they fit together.

film.headline: Start with the configuration items.
film.body: Servers, workstations and network devices form the terrain. SW tiles show software installed on servers.

film.headline: Follow the connections.
film.body: Multiple networks connect devices, while ICT systems group the components that support a capability.

film.headline: Connect to the purpose.
film.body: Mission services and business services depend on these systems and their recorded relationships.

sections.kicker: From an observation to a question
sections.title: Investigate an issue or finding
sections.lead: One device. Three leads to investigate.
body: Follow D3 from a software finding to an unmatched address and the services connected through its ICT system. Each observation raises a different question about the same terrain.

story.title: A finding gives you a starting point.
story.body: F-01 is recorded against software on D3. Check the finding, installed software and reporting source.

story.title: The same device reveals a gap.
story.body: D3 also communicates with 192.0.2.87, which has no matching endpoint record. Establish its identity and owner.

story.title: The record connects to service purpose.
story.body: D3 belongs to System B, supporting Mission service A and Business service B. Review the dependencies and service state.

story.title: Three leads. A clearer investigation.
story.body: Validate the finding, identify the unknown and review dependencies. These observations do not prove exploitation or an outage.

sections.title: Security Vulnerabilities
sections.lead: Locate the weakness. Understand what depends on it.
body: Vulnerabilities can affect devices and their installed software. TSAAT helps you inspect the affected device and the source that reported the finding.
Use the same cyber terrain to trace the affected device to its ICT system and dependent mission or business services. Validate exploitability and service impact before deciding on action.
sections.takeaway: Connect the finding to its asset, then validate the wider context.

options.label: Finding
options.title: Understand the observation
options.body: Start with the reported weakness and affected device. F-01 is an illustrative software finding; check the actual finding, reporting source and evidence.

options.label: Asset
options.title: Locate the affected component
options.body: Locate the marked device within its network. Its blue SW tile represents installed software. The device stays in the same position as in the Cyber Terrain view.

options.label: Context
options.title: Connect it to a decision
options.body: Highlight the device's ICT system and dependent mission or business services. The other devices stay visible for context. These relationships do not confirm exploitation or a service impact.

film.headline: A finding needs a place.
film.body: A recorded vulnerability is linked to an endpoint or installed software.

film.headline: A place needs context.
film.body: Look at the reporting source, asset details and recorded relationships.

film.headline: Context supports prioritisation.
film.body: Validate exploitability and service relevance before deciding on action.

sections.title: Shadow IT
sections.lead: An unknown address is a question to resolve.
body: Network observations can reveal an address with no match in known endpoint records. CMDB discovery scans can also detect an address without being able to classify its device type.
Explore the three scenarios below. Distinguish the observing device or discovery source from the unknown address, then investigate its identity, classification and ownership.
sections.takeaway: Keep the source and the unknown address separate. Validate identity, device type and ownership.

options.label: Endpoint observation
options.title: A known endpoint reports an address
options.body: D3 is the reporting endpoint in ICT System B. Its network observations include an address with no matching endpoint record.
options.revealedTitle: An unmatched address, separate from D3
options.revealedBody: 192.0.2.87 has no matching endpoint record. Check the observation, identity and owner. D3 is the known reporting device; it is not the unknown endpoint.

options.label: Network device communication
options.title: A network device communicates with an address
options.body: Known network device ND1 communicates with another address that has no matching endpoint record. Keep ND1 separate from the unmatched address.
options.revealedTitle: ND1 is known; the other address is unmatched
options.revealedBody: 198.51.100.64 is the unmatched address observed in ND1's communication. Check ND1's records and network context, then establish the other endpoint's identity and owner.

options.label: CMDB discovery scan
options.title: Discovery finds an address it cannot classify
options.body: CMDB discovery scans an IP range and detects 192.0.2.47, but cannot classify it as a Server, Computer, Printer or Router.
options.revealedBody: 192.0.2.47 was detected by the scan, but its device type is unclassified. Review discovery evidence and classification results; establish its type, identity and owner before assigning a class.

film.headline: An endpoint observes an unmatched address.
film.body: D3 reports communication with an address that has no matching endpoint record.

film.headline: A network device sees another unmatched address.
film.body: ND1 is the known network device. The other address is the one to investigate.

film.headline: Discovery finds an unclassified address.
film.body: A CMDB IP-range scan detects an address but cannot classify it as a Server, Computer, Printer or Router.

sections.title: Service Impacts
sections.lead: Follow a local issue to the services that may depend on it.
body: Mission and business services depend on ICT systems, their devices and software, and the networks connecting them. An issue in one component may be relevant to several services.

Use the same cyber terrain to explore a device issue or an unavailable device link. Follow the highlighted relationships to identify services to review, then confirm the actual impact with their owners.
sections.takeaway: Trace the dependency. Confirm what it means for the service.

options.label: Device D1
options.title: D1 to System A to business services
options.body: D1 belongs to ICT System A. Business services A and B depend on A, so review both. Business service B also depends on System B; validate those dependencies and the current service state.

options.label: Device D5
options.title: D5 to System C to mission services
options.body: D5 belongs to ICT System C. Mission services A and B depend on C, so review both. Mission service A also depends on System B; that relationship remains visible for context.

options.label: Device link
options.title: D7 to D3: two system contexts
options.body: The link between D7 in System A and D3 in System B is unavailable. Follow those endpoints to Business services A and B and Mission service A. Check alternative paths before confirming service impact.

film.headline: The same terrain. A different question.
film.body: Start with a device issue or an unavailable device link and trace its recorded dependencies.

film.headline: Identify the services to review.
film.body: ICT systems connect the starting issue to mission and business services. Highlighted services require investigation.

film.headline: Validate the impact.
film.body: Confirm dependencies, alternative paths and current service state with the service owner.

sections.title: Reporting and focused insights
sections.lead: Watch observations become a focused report.
body: Choose a scenario. Adjust scope or search, then pause or step through the result.
sections.takeaway: Choose the report whose scope matches your question.

options.label: Filtered Excel
options.title: Take every matching record with you
options.body: Export every row matching the current scope and Explorer search, chart or column filters, across all pages. This example uses one device per row; other explorers may show several rows for one device.

options.label: Briefing PDF
options.title: Brief the selected cyber terrain
options.body: Governance PDFs follow the briefing's applied header filters and loaded snapshot. Explorer filters do not narrow them. Change the example search to see the briefing count remain tied to its scope.

options.label: Impact PDF
options.title: Show the connections behind the question
options.body: In Topology Explorer, select a starting CI or all matching results, then a graph mode and layout. The PDF includes the full traced graph and supporting evidence. This example shows device, system and service relationships.

film.headline: Start with your view.
film.body: Start with the information available in your TSAAT view and the question you need to answer.

film.headline: Narrow the view.
film.body: Select cyber terrain and date, then check the loaded snapshot. Use relevant Discovery search and table filters.

film.headline: A focused answer.
film.body: Use Governance for scoped summaries and Discovery to inspect matching records. Choose the view that answers your question.

film.headline: Report with context.
film.body: Governance PDFs use header scope and snapshot. Explorer Excel exports matching filtered rows. Check what the download includes before sharing.

sections.title: TSAAT benefits
sections.lead: A clearer starting point for the next decision.
body: Bring asset records, relationships and findings into a common view. Move from a summary to the detail that supports it.
Use that view to investigate gaps, involve owners and report with traceable detail. Check the quality and currency of source records before drawing conclusions.
sections.takeaway: Understand the terrain, involve the right people and choose the next step.

film.headline: See a shared picture.
film.body: Bring assets, relationships and findings into one conversation.

film.headline: Ask a sharper question.
film.body: Move from a summary to the records that support it.

film.headline: Take the next step.
film.body: Investigate gaps, involve owners and report with clearer context.

timeline.title: Build the discovery foundation
timeline.body: OPORD/01-2019: HICTO initiates a project to establish a CMDB and dynamic discovery of Defence networks. An enterprise CMDB discovery platform is delivered for DPE and DSE by June 2022.

timeline.title: Establish configuration management
timeline.body: Configuration Management Processes are established, including ICT System Modelling.

timeline.title: Assess critical ICT systems
timeline.body: For the Defence Strategic Review (DSR), HICTO-directed orders 66 and 67 assess the threat surface area of approximately 87 critical ICT systems. Systems are assessed against 28 compliance questions and reported through TSAAT V1.0.

timeline.title: Scale the system picture
timeline.body: The Defence ICT Inventory System (DIIS) is created to record ICT systems across Defence networks and capture ownership details. OMWOW progresses modelling of approximately 3,000 ICT systems across the Defence cyber terrain. TSAAT V2.0 is released in Q4 2025, with training to support OMWOW.

timeline.title: Bring the terrain into focus
timeline.body: TSAAT is presented to DSOC and Cyber Command as a reporting tool to assist with visibility of the cyber terrain.

timeline.title: Design the next release
timeline.body: TSAAT V3.0 is designed to meet DSOC needs, with delivery planned for January 2027.

layers.label: All components
layers.description: See the complete illustrative topology: 18 device CIs across three networks, their ICT systems, and the mission and business services they support.

layers.label: Devices + software
layers.description: Orange nodes are device configuration items (CIs). Attached blue SW tiles show installed software on servers.

layers.label: Networks + relationships
layers.description: Highlight the devices and their network connections across Operations, Enterprise and Support. Moving dashed lines show communication between the devices and networks.

layers.label: ICT systems + services
layers.description: Highlight all 18 devices, their three ICT systems, and the mission and business services they support. Each service can depend on one or more ICT systems.

layers.label: Mission services
layers.description: Mission service A depends on Systems B and C. Mission service B depends on System C. Both services, their connected ICT systems and linked devices are highlighted.

layers.label: Business services
layers.description: Business service A depends on System A. Business service B depends on Systems A and B. Both services, their connected ICT systems and linked devices are highlighted.

benefits.title: Evidence in context

benefits.title: Clearer reporting
